concept.title: Ordered lists
concept.abstract: This section covers Ordered Lists in Markdown — items presented in a defined sequence where position is significant — and twenty-one scenarios grouped across six categories: consecutive and discontinuous numbered lists as procedures and workflows, single-item numbered lists, two-level and three-level nested numbered lists, and interrupted numbered lists where an admonition, paragraph, image, table, or bullet list appears between items. The converter maps each ordered list to <ol><li> in concept and reference topics, or to <steps><step><cmd> in task topics, based on the heading classification and content context.

conbody.p: An ordered list presents items in a defined sequence where the position of each item is significant. The ordered lists are universally used for step-by-step procedures, installation instructions, and ranked items.

For the reader, a numbered list communicates that sequence is contractual — item 2 depends on item 1 being completed, and performing the items out of order produces an incorrect or unsafe result. It is also a navigational reference that lets a reader say "I am on step 4" and return to the correct position after an interruption.
The list level is controlled by the Increase and Decrease Indent buttons, determines nesting depth: level 1 is the top level, level 2 is the first nested level, level 3 is the second, and so on.
conbody.note: The list level assigned by list controls is what drives the nesting structure in the DITA output.
conbody.p: A simple ordered list in Markdown is created by prefixing each item with a number followed by a period (.). For example:1. Install the application. 2. Configure the system settings. 3. Start the service. 4. Verify the installation.

The converter analyzes both the list structure and the surrounding content to determine the appropriate DITA output. Depending on the context, the same ordered list may represent either a procedural task or sequential reference information. Procedural content is converted into DITA task structures using <steps>, <step>, and <substeps>, while non-procedural sequential content is converted into DITA ordered lists (<ol>) within Concept or Reference topics. Supporting content, such as images, tables, and nested lists, is preserved according to the generated DITA structure.
The following scenarios demonstrate how different ordered list structures are interpreted during Markdown-to-DITA conversion and how they affect the generated DITA output.
